examples.solution_text:
(a) The ticks show $AB=AC$.
$BC$ has a different length, so exactly two sides are equal.
The triangle is isosceles.
(b) All three side lengths are different.
The triangle is scalene.

examples.question_text:
Classify each triangle by its angle properties.
(a) Angles of $53^{\circ}$, $58^{\circ}$ and $69^{\circ}$.
(b) Angles of $106^{\circ}$, $32^{\circ}$ and $42^{\circ}$.
examples.solution_text:
(a) The largest angle is $69^{\circ}$.
Every angle is less than $90^{\circ}$, so the triangle is acute-angled.
(b) $106^{\circ}>90^{\circ}$.
One angle is obtuse, so the triangle is obtuse-angled.

(a) Clockwise from $L$, the vertices are $L$, $K$, then $J$.
The triangle is $\Delta LKJ$.
(b) The matching ticks show $JK=KL$.
The opposite angles are equal: $\angle JLK=\angle LJK$.
(c) The square at $K$ marks a right angle.
The two equal sides meet at $K$, and the third side is different.
The triangle is isosceles and right-angled.
(d) The vertex opposite $JK$ is $L$.
The angle is $\angle JLK$.

examples.question_text:
(a) A triangle has angles $116^{\circ}$, $32^{\circ}$ and $32^{\circ}$. Explain how it shows that not every isosceles triangle is acute-angled.
(b) Can an equilateral triangle be right-angled or obtuse-angled? Give a reason.
examples.solution_text:
(a) The two $32^{\circ}$ angles are equal, so their opposite sides are equal.
The other angle is different, so the third side has a different length.
$116^{\circ}>90^{\circ}$, so the triangle is obtuse-angled.
This isosceles, obtuse-angled triangle shows the claim is false.
(b) All three angles of an equilateral triangle are $60^{\circ}$.
Every angle is less than $90^{\circ}$, so it is always acute-angled.
It cannot be right-angled or obtuse-angled.

(a) All three sides have matching ticks, so the triangle is equilateral.
Its three angles are $60^{\circ}$, so it is also acute-angled.
(b) All three angles are different, so their opposite sides are different. The triangle is scalene.
The largest angle is $75^{\circ}<90^{\circ}$, so it is also acute-angled.

examples.question_text: Leah calls a triangle with sides $7\text{ cm}$, $7\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$ equilateral. Is Leah correct? Give the correct side classification.
examples.solution_text:
An equilateral triangle has three equal sides.
Two sides are $7\text{ cm}$, but the third is $10\text{ cm}$.
Leah is incorrect: exactly two sides are equal, so the triangle is isosceles.

examples.derivation: (a) The diagram has three matching side ticks. Its base length is 3; each sloping side has length sqrt(1.5² + 2.598076²), approximately 3. It is equilateral, with three 60° angles, hence acute-angled. (b) 48° + 57° + 75° = 180°. All angles differ, so all opposite sides differ: scalene. The largest angle, 75°, is below 90°, so it is acute-angled. These methods follow the supplied side-properties teaching and Foundation classification exercises.

7 + 7 > 10, so the lengths define a triangle. Exactly two lengths equal 7 cm; the third is 10 cm. The triangle is isosceles, and Leah's equilateral classification is incorrect.
